user.text: Add view transitions to this product gallery app. When navigating from the grid to a product detail page, the product image should smoothly morph between the thumbnail and the large detail image using a shared element transition. Page navigations should slide directionally. Suspense loading states should transition smoothly from skeleton to content. All animations must respect the user's prefers-reduced-motion preference.

history.assistant:
I added view transitions using React's <ViewTransition> and the <Link transitionTypes> prop, following the Next.js guide in node_modules/next/dist/docs/01-app/02-guides/view-transitions.md. The build passes and both pages load, but I haven't watched the animations in a browser.

Image morph (app/ProductGrid.tsx, app/product/[slug]/page.tsx): The grid thumbnail and the detail image both use the name product-image-${slug}. On the detail page I kept the large image outside the <Suspense> boundary so it appears at the same moment as the navigation. Without that, the thumbnail has nothing to morph into, and the large image would just fade in instead.

Sliding between pages (new file app/DirectionalTransition.tsx): Both pages are wrapped in this component. Links from the grid slide forward; the "← Back to products" link slides back. It goes in each page rather than the shared layout, because the layout doesn't re-render on navigation and so wouldn't animate. The browser's own back button doesn't get the slide, but the image morph still runs.

Loading states: On both pages the skeleton slides down and fades out quickly, then the real content slides up and fades in.

app/globals.css:
- The animation styles for all three effects.
- Clicks still reach the page while an animation is running.
- When the user has reduced motion turned on, all transition animations are switched off, and so is the skeleton's pulsing.

No config change was needed. Your package.json lists React 19.1, but Next ships its own React 19.3, which already includes these APIs.

Checks:
- npx tsc --noEmit -p .: passed (exit 0).
- npm run build: compiled and generated all routes.
- next start with curl: / and /product/classic-sneakers both returned 200, and the product name rendered.

next build also changed tsconfig.json on its own, adding .next/dev/types//.ts to include.

2  	title: Designing view transitions
3  	description: Learn how to use view transitions to communicate meaning during navigation, loading, and content changes in a Next.js app.
4  	nav_title: View transitions
5  	---
6  	
7  	In web apps, route changes replace the entire page at once. One set of elements disappears, another appears, with no visual connection between them. A user selects a photo thumbnail to view it in detail on another page. They are the same image, but nothing on screen communicates that.
8  	
9  	Apps that need these transitions typically rely on complex animation libraries that manage mount/unmount lifecycles, track element positions across routes, and coordinate timing manually, to animate how elements enter, exit, and move between states.
10 	
11 	React's `<ViewTransition>` component integrates with the browser's [View Transitions API](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/View_Transition_API) to handle this declaratively. You name the elements that should persist, and the browser animates between their old and new positions.
12 	
13 	This guide walks through four patterns that cover the most common cases: morphing shared elements, animating loading states, adding directional navigation, and crossfading content within the same route.
14 	
15 	## Add view transitions with an agent
16 	
17 	The [`vercel-react-view-transitions`](https://skills.sh/vercel-labs/agent-skills/vercel-react-view-transitions) skill teaches a coding agent the patterns in this guide, plus the CSS recipes and troubleshooting for applying them to an existing app.
18 	
19 	Install the skill:
20 	
21 	```bash filename="Terminal"
22 	npx skills add vercel-labs/agent-skills --skill vercel-react-view-transitions
23 	```
24 	
25 	Then prompt the agent with something like:
26 	
27 	```prompt
28 	Add view transitions to this app using the vercel-react-view-transitions skill.
29 	```
30 	
31 	Or prompt for a specific transition, such as:
32 	
33 	- Morphing a thumbnail into a hero image
34 	- Sliding between routes forward and back
35 	- Crossfading content within the same route
36 	
37 	To apply the patterns yourself, follow the walkthrough below.
38 	
39 	## Example
40 	
41 	As an example, we'll build a photography gallery called _Frames_.
42 	
43 	We'll start by morphing a thumbnail into a hero image (shared elements), then animate the loading skeleton into real content (Suspense reveals), add directional slides for forward and back navigation (route transitions), and finish with crossfades for switching between photographer tabs (same-route transitions).
44 	
45 	You can find the resources used in this example here:
46 	
47 	- [Demo](https://react-view-transitions-demo.labs.vercel.dev)
48 	- [Code](https://github.com/vercel-labs/react-view-transitions-demo)
49 	
50 	View transitions work in the App Router with no configuration. React 19.3 includes the `<ViewTransition>` component and `addTransitionType` API used in this guide.
51 	
52 	> [!NOTE]
53 	> React's integration uses newer View Transitions API features (transition types and `view-transition-class`), available in Chromium 125+ and recent Safari and Firefox versions. Some animations may behave differently in Safari. Without browser support, your application works normally; the transitions do not animate.
54 	
55 	Import the `ViewTransition` component from React:
56 	
57 	```tsx
58 	import { ViewTransition } from 'react'
59 	```
60 	
61 	`<ViewTransition>` animations are activated by [Transitions](https://react.dev/reference/react/useTransition), [`<Suspense>`](https://react.dev/reference/react/Suspense), and [`useDeferredValue`](https://react.dev/reference/react/useDeferredValue). Regular `setState` calls do not trigger them. In Next.js, route navigations are transitions, so `<ViewTransition>` animations activate automatically during navigation.

103 104 ) 105 } 106 ``` 107 108 The `name` prop creates identity. React finds elements with the same name on the old and new pages, then animates between their size and position automatically. No additional props are needed for the morph to work. 109 110 If we click a thumbnail now, the image scales and repositions from its grid cell to the hero slot. Navigating back reverses the morph. The user sees one object moving, not two objects swapping. 111 112 The morph plays when the destination content renders in the same commit as the navigation, which is the case with prefetched (cached) pages. If the destination suspends into a fallback first, no pair forms, and the content animates with its enter animation instead when it arrives. 113 114 #### Customizing the morph animation 115 116 The morph works without any CSS. To customize it, add `share="morph"` together with `default="none"`. The `share` prop assigns the `morph` class to the view transition, which you can target with CSS pseudo-elements. For example, to soften the morph mid-flight with a [`blur`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/filter-function/blur) keyframe: 117 118 ```tsx 119 120 121 122 ``` 123 124 Add the same props to both Step 1 snippets (`photo-grid.tsx` and `photo-content.tsx`). `default="none"` keeps each named image from running its own crossfade on every unrelated transition. Without it, every named `` animates whenever any transition runs on the page. When you add `default="none"` to a named pair, keep the explicit `share`. With `default="none"` and no `share` prop, the pair silently stops morphing. 125 126 ```css filename="app/globals.css" 127 ::view-transition-group(.morph) { 128 animation-duration: 400ms; 129 } 130 ::view-transition-image-pair(.morph) { 131 animation-name: via-blur; 132 } 133 @keyframes via-blur { 134 30% { 135 filter: blur(3px); 136 } 137 } 138 ``` 139 140 The blur hides pixel-level interpolation artifacts during the transition. At 400ms, the morph is slow enough to register but fast enough to feel direct. 141 142 ### Step 2: Animate loading states with Suspense reveals 143 144 The photo detail page loads its content asynchronously. While data is in flight, a Suspense boundary shows a skeleton. When the data resolves, the skeleton is replaced by the real content. 145 146 Without a transition, the swap is instant. The skeleton vanishes and the content pops in. 147 148 In motion design, vertical direction encodes hierarchy. Content sliding up communicates arrival. Content sliding down communicates departure. The pair together creates a handoff: the placeholder yields to the real thing. 149 150 Wrap the Suspense fallback in a `ViewTransition` with an exit animation, and the content in a `ViewTransition` with an enter animation: 151 152 ```tsx filename="app/photo/[id]/page.tsx" 153 import { Suspense, ViewTransition } from 'react' 154 155 export default async function PhotoPage({ params }) { 156 const { id } = await params 157 158 return ( 159 162 163 164 } 165 > 166 167 168 169 170 ) 171 } 172 ``` 173 174 As in Step 1, `default="none"` prevents this `ViewTransition` from animating during unrelated transitions, like the shared element morph. 175 176 The CSS animations use asymmetric timing. The exit is fast (150ms). The enter fade is slower (210ms) and delayed until the exit completes, while its slide movement runs longer (400ms): 177 178 ```css filename="app/globals.css" 179 :root { 180 --duration-exit: 150ms; 181 --duration-enter: 210ms; 182 --duration-move: 400ms; 183 } 184 185 ::view-transition-old(.slide-down) { 186 animation: 187 var(--duration-exit) ease-out both fade reverse, 188 var(--duration-exit) ease-out both slide-y reverse; 189 } 190 ::view-transition-new(.slide-up) { 191 animation: 192 var(--duration-enter) ease-in var(--duration-exit) both fade, 193 var(--duration-move) ease-in both slide-y; 194 } 195 196 @keyframes fade { 197 from { 198 filter: blur(3px); 199 opacity: 0; 200 } 201 to { 202 filter: blur(0); 203 opacity: 1; 204 } 205 } 206 @keyframes slide-y { 207 from { 208 transform: translateY(10px); 209 } 210 to { 211 transform: translateY(0); 212 } 213 } 214 ``` 215 216 The asymmetry is deliberate. Old content should leave quickly so it does not compete for attention. New content should arrive more gently so the user has time to register it. The `var(--duration-exit)` delay on the enter fade means the new content waits for the old content to finish leaving before it becomes visible. 217 218 If we refresh the page, the skeleton slides down and fades out, and a moment later the real content slides up and fades in. 219 220 ### Step 3: Add directional motion for navigation 221 222 The gallery now has morphing images and animated loading states. But navigating between pages still has no directional signal. Forward and back navigations look identical. The user cannot tell from the animation whether they moved deeper into the app or returned to a previous page. 223 224 In film and animation, horizontal direction encodes spatial position. Moving left means progressing forward (like turning a page in a left-to-right language). Moving right means going back. This convention is so ingrained that violating it feels disorienting. 225 226 Use the `transitionTypes` prop on `` to tag forward navigations: 227 228 ```tsx filename="components/photo-grid.tsx" 229 230 {/* photo thumbnail */} 231 232 ``` 233 234 The same pattern works for any navigation within the app. For example, previous/next arrows on a photo detail page can use `nav-back` and `nav-forward` to animate in the corresponding direction. 235 236 For links that return the user to a previous page, use `nav-back`: 237 238 ```tsx filename="app/photo/[id]/page.tsx" 239 240 ← Gallery 241 242 ``` 243 244 The transition type is not automatic.
